Mastra C2 beacon: node.exe to Hostwinds 23.254.164.92:8000 / .123:443 AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the setup.cjs dropper or its second-stage tasking client connecting to the attacker-controlled Hostwinds infrastructure used by the Mastra campaign. Single-event alerting on the two confirmed C2 IPs. Rationale: Two attacker-controlled IPs (23.254.164.92:8000 fetch, 23.254.164.123:443 beacon) and two Hostwinds DNS names published verbatim by Microsoft Threat Intelligence. Single-IOC match is high-fidelity because the IPs sit on a low-reputation hosting provider and were freshly stood up for this campaign. The DNS join catches detections even when the proxy resolves IPs locally. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105 T1571
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal threat-intel sandbox or red team detonating the dropper for research
  • Security researcher pivoting against the Hostwinds IP space from a corporate host
  • A different legitimate Hostwinds-hosted customer reusing the same IP after take-down (low — IPs were burned)
  • DNS scanner / passive DNS collector hitting the hwsrv-132778x hostnames
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node","npm.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") or isempty(InitiatingProcessFileName)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process (expect node.exe), pull bytes-up/down to gauge whether the second-stage payload was retrieved or implant beacons completed; enrich the IP via passive DNS for any other Hostwinds C2 names. 2) Contain: block 23.254.164.0/24 at the egress proxy / firewall, sinkhole the two hwsrv-132778[56].hostwindsdns.com domains, isolate any host that connected. 3) Hunt: pivot on the source host to UC1 (setup.cjs execution), UC3 (NvmProtocal Run key), UC5 (wallet/browser data access); broaden lookback to 30d to catch any earlier connection from CI runners.
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where RemoteIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | where RemotePort in (8000, 443)
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256),
(DeviceEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType == "DnsQueryResponse"
  | where AdditionalFields has_any ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, AdditionalFields, InitiatingProcessFileName)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(CommonSecurityLog
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DestinationIP in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, DeviceVendor, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication),
(DnsEvents
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Name in~ ("hwsrv-1327785.hostwindsdns.com","hwsrv-1327786.hostwindsdns.com")
  | project TimeGenerated, Computer, ClientIP, Name, QueryType),
(ImNetworkSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DstIpAddr in ("23.254.164.92","23.254.164.123")
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant Windows persistence: NvmProtocal Run key + NodePackages drop AIInstallation High
Detects the cross-platform tasking implant installing login persistence on Windows by writing the NvmProtocal value under HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run and/or dropping protocal.cjs under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\. Rationale: Microsoft Table 2 names the persistence artifact 'NvmProtocal' (note the typo — 'Protocal' vs 'Protocol') under C:\ProgramData\NodePackages\ — both strings are unique enough that any hit is essentially confirmed malicious. The typo is a high-fidelity anchor because legitimate NVM uses 'Protocol' or no such key at all. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/mastra-ai/mastra/issues/18046
ATT&CKT1547.001 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A user installs a legitimate NVM4W variant that coincidentally writes a similarly named key (extremely unlikely with the 'Protocal' typo)
  • Security tooling re-detonating the implant in an analysis VM
  • Forensic acquisition tooling reading the key (would show ActionType=RegistryQuery, not Set/Created — already filtered)
  • Manual analyst remediation activity touching the path after IR is underway
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe","msiexec.exe") or RegistryValueData has "protocal.cjs"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the value data to confirm it points at protocal.cjs; correlate to the initiating process (expect node.exe, sometimes powershell.exe); hash protocal.cjs and compare against the published five SHA256s. 2) Contain: isolate the host, delete the Run value and the NodePackages folder, kill the implant process, rotate any credentials/tokens/cookies accessible to that user. 3) Hunt: query ImageLoadEvents / DllInjection for reflective .NET loads from node.exe in the prior 24h; check for the equivalent macOS LaunchAgent ~/Library/NodePackages/com.nvm.protocal.plist and Linux ~/.config/systemd/nvmconf/nvmconf.service across the fleet.
union
(DeviceRegistryEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where ActionType in ("RegistryValueSet","RegistryKeyCreated")
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValueName =~ "NvmProtocal"
        or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName),
(DeviceFileEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(14d)
  | where FileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or FolderPath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine)
| sort by Timestamp desc
union isfuzzy=true
(ImRegistryEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where RegistryKey has @"\CurrentVersion\Run"
  | where RegistryValue =~ "NvmProtocal" or RegistryValueData has_any (@"\ProgramData\NodePackages\", "protocal.cjs")
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, RegistryKey, RegistryValue, RegistryValueData, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine),
(ImFileEvent
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where TargetFileName =~ "protocal.cjs" or TargetFilePath has @"\ProgramData\NodePackages\"
  | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256)
| sort by TimeGenerated desc

Mastra implant credential access: node.exe reading crypto wallet extensions / browser History AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the second-stage tasking implant inventorying the 166 cryptocurrency wallet browser-extension IDs and copying browser History/Login Data into temp paths prefixed with 'browser-hist-'. Non-browser Node.js process touching browser profile data is the key signal. Rationale: Article confirms node.exe inventories 166 wallet extension IDs across Chrome/Edge/Brave profiles, copies History SQLite into temp paths prefixed 'browser-hist-' (verbatim). Non-browser process reading browser secret stores is normally rare; the node.exe-as-initiator pivot makes this a tight detection on developer endpoints.
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005 T1217
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Electron-based developer tools (VS Code extensions, GitHub Desktop, Slack desktop) reading their own Chromium profile under User Data — distinguish via the Local Extension Settings/History/Login Data sub-paths
  • Browser-history exporters (e.g. browsing-history-export CLI) that some devs run via node
  • Backup/sync tools written in Node that snapshot the browser profile
  • Penetration-testing tooling on engagement laptops
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("Code.exe","code.exe","GitHubDesktop.exe","slack.exe","Teams.exe","Discord.exe") and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\AppData\Local\Programs\Microsoft VS Code\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the parent of node.exe (expect npm postinstall lineage from UC1, not VS Code / Electron); enumerate which extension IDs / which browser profile were touched; check for outbound POSTs to UC2 IPs within 5 minutes of the access. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate node tree, rotate seed phrases / hardware-wallet PINs / exchange API keys / 2FA seeds for every wallet found, expire all browser sessions for that user. 3) Hunt: correlate the user's Okta/Entra sign-ins and CEX exchange logins for the prior 7d; check for fund-movement events; pivot to UC2 for exfil confirmation and any HTTPS POST with the legacy IE8 User-Agent.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where (FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                              @"\User Data\Default\History",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                              @"\User Data\Default\Cookies",
                              @"\Brave-Browser\User Data\",
                              @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\"))
   or FileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where ActingProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Local Extension Settings\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Extensions\",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\History",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Login Data",
                                  @"\User Data\Default\Cookies")
   or TargetFileName startswith "browser-hist-"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:11 @Image:(*\\node.exe OR *\\Node.exe) (@TargetFilename:(*\\User\ Data\\Default\\Local\ Extension\ Settings\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Extensions\\* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\History* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Login\ Data* OR *\\User\ Data\\Default\\Cookies*) OR @TargetFilename:*\\browser-hist-*)
#event_simpleName=FileOpenInfo ContextImageFileName=/\\node\.exe$/i (TargetFileName=/\\User Data\\.*\\(Local Extension Settings|Extensions|History|Login Data|Cookies)/i OR TargetFileName=/\\browser-hist-/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

Mastra implant discovery: PowerShell child of node.exe running Get-StartApps / Get-AppxPackage AIActions on Objectives High
Detects the implant's host-fingerprinting step: enumerating installed software via Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, and registry Uninstall keys in rapid succession spawned as a child of node.exe. Rationale: Microsoft's Phase 6 reconstruction names the exact three enumeration mechanisms (Get-StartApps, Get-AppxPackage, registry Uninstall) used by the implant for victim profiling. PowerShell as a child of node.exe is rare in normal developer use; combined with these three discovery commands, this is essentially confirmation of the implant being active.
ATT&CKT1518 T1518.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An npm package's postinstall that legitimately queries installed apps via PowerShell (rare but exists for some Windows-targeting npm modules)
  • node-based system inventory tools (e.g. systeminformation library wrappers) that shell out for AppX data
  • DevOps tooling that uses node to drive PowerShell-based Windows configuration checks
  • Electron app updater that queries Get-AppxPackage to detect Store-installed versions
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "systeminformation" and InitiatingProcessParentFileName !in~ ("electron.exe","Code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and parent node.exe command line; check if setup.cjs or a randomly named .js was the parent (UC1 lineage); look at the next 60 seconds of process events on the same host for follow-on PS reading browser data or registry hives. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill node and powershell trees, quarantine any .js dropped under temp/AppData. 3) Hunt: pivot on UC2 (C2 IPs) and UC5 (wallet/browser access) for the same DeviceId; check whether the user has any privileged AD / cloud roles and freeze them pending review.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("node.exe","node")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| sort by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\node.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith "\\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Get-StartApps","Get-AppxPackage",@"\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Uninstall")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count

File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match Installation High
Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or SHA1 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf") or MD5 in~ ("b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["b122a9873bedf145ae2a7fd024b5f309007dbb025149f4dc4ac3f7e4f32a36a4", "c38954e85bf5433e61e7c8f4230336695624ae88b6953afabf7bf817aa91b638", "cdec8b20338beb708b5be8d3d7a3041a35a8b0fb92f9186262f312d55ff82066", "9570f77a5e1511869f4e554e7166df9fde081f2583e293c2569621792ed7d9c9", "221c45a790dec2a296af57969e1165a16f8f49733aeab64c0bbd768d9943badf"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control

Microsoft Security Blog
2026-06-17 12 use cases 15 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

Microsoft Threat Intelligence analyzed a cryptocurrency clipper campaign that combines clipboard theft, wallet replacement, Tor-based communications, and worm-like propagation. Beyond stealing cryptocurrency transactions, the malware establishes persistent access and enables follow-on activity through a lightweight backdoor capability. The post Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control appeared first on Microsoft Security Blog .

Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.

Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] CryptoBandits cfile payload artifact created under Public\Documents
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Crypto Clipper uses Tor and worm-like propagation for persistence and control
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] CryptoBandits scheduled task creation via XML import to Public\Documents 5-char staging folder · [LLM] WScript or CScript executing JavaScript payload from Public\Documents 5-char staging folder · [LLM] Renamed Tor client running as ugate.exe (CryptoBandits bundled proxy) · [LLM] Defender exclusion path added for Public\Documents staging folder (worm self-protection) · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Curl over Tor SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:9050 to .onion C2 · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] WScript or CScript with Public\Documents JS spawning curl, schtasks, cmd, or PowerShell child
CryptoBandits scheduled task creation via XML import to Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects the worm/stealer persistence step where schtasks.exe imports a task definition XML from a 5-character subfolder of C:\Users\Public\Documents. This is the exact persistence shape Microsoft published for CryptoBandits.A and is not produced by legitimate scheduled-task workflows. Rationale: Article code block 1 ships this exact regex verbatim — schtasks.exe + /create + /xml pointing into a [a-z]{4,6} subfolder of Public\Documents is the published CryptoBandits persistence signature and has effectively zero legitimate cause.
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1547
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Enterprise software-distribution tools that stage tasks via XML in Public\Documents (rare)
  • IT scripts that import scheduled tasks for shared workstations from a public staging share
  • Backup/imaging utilities that recreate scheduled tasks during post-deploy
  • Custom developer test harnesses validating schtasks /xml syntax
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine, the XML file at the referenced path (Defender DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath), and the parent that spawned schtasks.exe — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent is high confidence CryptoBandits. 2) Contain: isolate the device with MDE Live Response, terminate any ugate.exe / wscript.exe with parents in Public\Documents, and pull the XML + the JS payloads from the staging folder. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl with --socks5-hostname, cfile under Public\Documents, Defender exclusion adds, and look for the same 5-character folder pattern on other endpoints (USB worm spread).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: CryptoBandits Scheduled Task Import From Public Documents 5-char Folder
id: 6b9a4d1f-3c0e-4a2b-8e1a-cf2e3b6d9011
description: Detects schtasks.exe importing an XML task definition from a 5-6 character subfolder of C:\Users\Public\Documents, the persistence shape used by the CryptoBandits clipper worm.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|re|i: 'schtasks\s+/create\s+/tn\s+[a-z]{4,6}\s+/xml\s+C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml\s+/f'
  condition: selection
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @Image:(*\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*"\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"* AND *"/create"* AND *"/xml"* AND *".xml"*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml/i
| CommandLine=/\/create/i
| CommandLine=/\/xml/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, UserName, CommandLine, ParentBaseFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.process="*/xml*" by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| rex field=process "(?i)/tn\s+(?<task_name>[a-z]{4,6})\s+/xml\s+(?<xml_path>C:\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\Documents\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml)"
| where isnotnull(task_name) AND isnotnull(xml_path)
| convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe Processes.process="*\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\*" Processes.process="*/create*" Processes.process="*/xml*" by host Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| rex field=process "(?i)/tn\s+(?<task_name>[a-z]{4,6})\s+/xml\s+(?<xml_path>C:\\\\Users\\\\Public\\\\Documents\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\\\\[a-z]{4,6}\.xml)"
| where isnotnull(task_name) AND isnotnull(xml_path)
| convert ctime(firstTime), ctime(lastTime)
Curl over Tor SOCKS5 proxy at localhost:9050 to .onion C2 AICommand & Control High
Detects curl.exe being driven through the bundled Tor SOCKS5 proxy at 127.0.0.1:9050 with an .onion destination on the command line. This is the canonical C2 invocation shape for the CryptoBandits clipper /route.php, /recvf.php, and /stub.php endpoints. Rationale: Lifted from article code blocks 2 and 3 — curl.exe with --socks5-hostname localhost:9050 AND a .onion target on the same command line is unique to the malware's documented C2 flow; no legitimate Windows admin workflow co-locates these three tokens.
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001 T1572
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power user manually running a curl-over-Tor command to test the local SOCKS5 listener
  • Red-team C2 tooling using the same Tor SOCKS5 pattern in an authorised exercise
  • Researcher fetching darknet IOC feeds via local Tor client
  • Privacy-conscious user driving curl through Tor Browser's SOCKS port
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("tor.exe", "tor-browser.exe", "firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessFileName — a wscript.exe/cscript.exe parent from C:\Users\Public\Documents is high confidence; capture the full .onion URL for IR notes. 2) Contain: isolate via MDE Live Response, kill curl.exe and any ugate.exe process, and block outbound 127.0.0.1:9050 path is moot — block the parent script and quarantine its folder. 3) Hunt: across the org look for ugate.exe, schtasks.exe importing XML from Public\Documents 5-char folders, cfile creation, and Defender exclusions for that path; treat any second host with the same 5-char folder name as part of the same USB-worm cluster.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName =~ "curl.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
| where CommandLine has_all ("--socks5-hostname", "localhost:9050", ".onion")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WScript or CScript executing JavaScript payload from Public\Documents 5-char staging folder AIInstallation High
Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe running a .js file inside the C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js path layout the CryptoBandits worm drops. This is the runtime entry point for the clipper/stealer component that polls the Tor C2. Rationale: Article describes JS payloads dropped to C:\Users\Public\Documents\<5char>\<5char>.js (example given: 'omoho' folder) and executed by Windows Script Host; this combination of path and script host fires only on CryptoBandits-shaped activity.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Endpoint-management agent dropping a one-off JS troubleshooting script to Public\Documents
  • MSP automation pushing .js fixes through a shared documents path
  • Custom in-house deployment tool using Public\Documents as a staging directory
  • Pentester or red-team operator simulating WSH-based persistence in the same path
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the .js file's SHA256 from DeviceFileEvents on FolderPath has 'Public\\Documents' and detonate in a sandbox or strings-scan for 'route.php', 'EVAL', 'SEED', 'PKEY'. 2) Contain: kill wscript.exe / cscript.exe with these arguments, quarantine the 5-char folder, and remove the matching scheduled tasks from UC1. 3) Hunt: pivot on the device for ugate.exe execution, curl --socks5-hostname, cfile drops, and the originating .lnk on removable media (DeviceFileEvents FileName endswith '.lnk' and FolderPath matches '^[D-Z]:\\').
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)C:\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\[a-z]{4,6}\\[a-z]{4,6}\.js"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Renamed Tor client running as ugate.exe (CryptoBandits bundled proxy) AIInstallation High
Detects execution of a binary literally named ugate.exe — the article's exact name for the renamed Tor proxy that the clipper launches to bootstrap its hidden-service C2. Pair with the binary's location and parent to triage. Rationale: Article names the renamed Tor binary verbatim ('ugate.exe') and notes it is run hidden to bootstrap the hidden-service C2; no legitimate software ships an executable by this name.
ATT&CKT1036.005 T1090.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal app coincidentally named ugate.exe (very unlikely — verify FolderPath and SHA256 first)
  • Red-team operator simulating a renamed Tor client during an authorised test
  • Penetration-testing kit shipping Tor under the same masquerade name
  • Forensics or training lab analysing the same sample on a sanctioned VM
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\Users\\Public\\" or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "\\AppData\\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull FolderPath, SHA256 and the parent process — a wscript.exe parent from Public\Documents is conclusive; submit the hash to the AV cloud and check Defender threat name for CryptoBandits.A. 2) Contain: isolate the device, terminate ugate.exe and its parent script host, and quarantine the binary plus the 5-char staging folder. 3) Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents for InitiatingProcessFileName == 'ugate.exe' to surface the C2, search across the org for the same SHA256, and check DeviceFileEvents for cfile and the JS payloads.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "ugate.exe"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\ugate.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Defender exclusion path added for Public\Documents staging folder (worm self-protection) AIInstallation High
Detects the CryptoBandits worm's self-protection step where it adds a Microsoft Defender Antivirus exclusion for its C:\Users\Public\Documents staging path before dropping JavaScript payloads. Covers both PowerShell Add-MpPreference and direct registry writes to the Defender exclusion key. Rationale: Article highlights Behavior:Win64/PathExclusion.ST detections and describes the worm excluding its staging folder before dropping payloads; the path string 'Public\Documents' combined with Add/Set-MpPreference + ExclusionPath is article-specific.
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1112
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP/RMM agent excluding Public\Documents because tenant uses it as a software-drop staging area
  • Sysadmin troubleshooting a Defender false positive on a shared workstation
  • Build farm or VDI gold-image script disabling AV scanning of staging directories
  • Endpoint security baseline tool reapplying a curated exclusion list
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("sccm.exe", "ccmexec.exe", "sense.exe", "intunemanagementextension.exe", "smc.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture InitiatingProcessFileName + parent chain — a wscript.exe / cmd.exe parent (not Intune/SCCM/admin shell) makes this CryptoBandits; check whether the exclusion is still active via 'Get-MpPreference | select ExclusionPath'. 2) Contain: remove the exclusion ('Remove-MpPreference -ExclusionPath ...'), isolate the host, and run a full Defender scan over Public\Documents. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC3 (wscript launching .js from the now-unexcluded path), UC4 (ugate.exe), and UC1 (schtasks XML import). Hash-collect anything new found under Public\Documents subfolders.
let ExclusionByPS = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where ProcessCommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where ProcessCommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
let ExclusionByRegistry = DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValueName has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
   or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValueName, " = ", RegistryValueData), InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by Timestamp desc
let ExclusionByPS = SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("Add-MpPreference", "Set-MpPreference")
| where CommandLine has "ExclusionPath"
| where CommandLine has @"Public\Documents"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, Source = "PowerShell", Detail = CommandLine, ParentProcessName;
let ExclusionByRegistry = ImRegistryEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Microsoft\Windows Defender\Exclusions\Paths"
| where RegistryValue has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" or RegistryValueData has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer = DvcHostname, SubjectUserName = ActorUsername, Source = "Registry", Detail = strcat(RegistryValue, " = ", RegistryValueData), ParentProcessName = ActingProcessName;
union ExclusionByPS, ExclusionByRegistry
| order by TimeGenerated desc

CryptoBandits cfile payload artifact created under Public\Documents AIDelivery High
Detects creation of a file literally named cfile under C:\Users\Public\Documents — the article-specific artifact where the clipper stores attacker-supplied code downloaded from the Tor C2 /stub.php endpoint and later invoked via the EVAL command. Rationale: Article explicitly names the on-disk artifact: 'A file named "cfile" is created on the infected system as an output for payload hosted on the C2 domain' and ties it to the EVAL remote-code-execution path — high-fidelity host-side IOC for active EVAL tasking.
ATT&CKT1105 T1059.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer creating a file legitimately named cfile in Public\Documents (extremely rare)
  • Cross-platform configuration tool dropping a generic cfile artifact
  • Custom in-house script using cfile as a temporary write target
  • Forensic analyst restoring the sample during a sanctioned investigation
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture SHA256 and contents of cfile (it should be JScript) — strings-scan for ActiveXObject, WScript.Shell, eval; pull InitiatingProcessFileName to see which wscript.exe / ugate.exe-tied process wrote it. 2) Contain: isolate the host, terminate the writing process tree, and quarantine cfile plus the surrounding 5-char folder. 3) Hunt: this is evidence of an active EVAL session — search DeviceProcessEvents on the same host for any new child processes spawned by wscript.exe in the 60 minutes around the cfile write and treat anything novel as attacker-supplied code.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FileName =~ "cfile"
| where FolderPath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventType =~ "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "cfile"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc

WScript or CScript with Public\Documents JS spawning curl, schtasks, cmd, or PowerShell child AIActions on Objectives High
Correlates the CryptoBandits JS loader (wscript.exe / cscript.exe whose command line points into C:\Users\Public\Documents) with its hands-on follow-on tooling: curl.exe (Tor exfil), schtasks.exe (persistence), cmd.exe / powershell.exe (EVAL backdoor execution). Each spawned child plus this parent is essentially an in-the-clear backdoor session. Rationale: Article maps the EVAL command to runtime JScript execution, then schedules persistence via schtasks and uses curl for Tor exfiltration — anchoring on a wscript/cscript parent whose command line still references Public\Documents .js + any of those four children is the cleanest chain signature.
ATT&CKT1059.007 T1059.001 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WSH-based deployment script under Public\Documents launching schtasks (uncommon — verify the JS file)
  • Vendor support utility scripted in JS that spawns curl for telemetry uploads
  • RMM/automation tool running JS workflows that shell out to PowerShell
  • Internal red-team simulation reusing this exact parent-child chain
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !has @"\Program Files (x86)\"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull both the parent (wscript/cscript) and child command lines — note the .js path and any curl --socks5-hostname or schtasks /xml arguments; capture the parent's full process tree from MDE. 2) Contain: isolate, kill the parent process and all descendants, quarantine the JS file and any spawned cfile or scheduled-task XML. 3) Hunt: pivot the parent JS SHA256 across the org, expand to UC4 (ugate.exe), and review DeviceFileEvents for .lnk files written to removable drives by the same parent — that uncovers the USB worm propagation step.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("wscript.exe", "cscript.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\"
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has ".js"
| where FileName in~ ("curl.exe", "schtasks.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or ParentProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("curl.exe", "schtasks.exe", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe")
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\curl.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith @"\pwsh.exe"
| join kind=inner (
    SecurityEvent
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
    | where EventID == 4688
    | where NewProcessName endswith @"\wscript.exe" or NewProcessName endswith @"\cscript.exe"
    | where CommandLine has @"\Users\Public\Documents\" and CommandLine has ".js"
    | project ParentPid = NewProcessId, ParentCmd = CommandLine, ParentName = NewProcessName, ParentHost = Computer
) on $left.ProcessId == $right.ParentPid and $left.Computer == $right.ParentHost
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, ParentCmd
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: WSH Script From Public Documents Spawning Curl Schtasks Or Shells (CryptoBandits Backdoor)
id: a72f8c3d-4e91-4b0a-9f3c-bd4e7a82f561
description: Detects wscript.exe or cscript.exe — driven by a JS payload from C:\Users\Public\Documents — spawning curl.exe, schtasks.exe, cmd.exe or powershell.exe. This is the in-the-clear chain of the CryptoBandits Tor backdoor's EVAL and tasking workflow.
references:
  - https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/06/17/crypto-clipper-uses-tor-worm-like-propagation-for-persistence-control/
author: thn-usecases
date: 2026/06/18
tags:

  - attack.t1059.007
  - attack.t1059.001
  - attack.t1059.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\wscript.exe'
      - '\cscript.exe'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '\Users\Public\Documents\'
    ParentCommandLine|contains: '.js'
  child:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\curl.exe'
      - '\schtasks.exe'
      - '\cmd.exe'
      - '\powershell.exe'
      - '\pwsh.exe'
  condition: parent and child
level: high
source:(windows.sysmon OR windows.security) (@EventID:1 OR @EventID:4688) @ParentImage:(*\wscript.exe OR *\WScript.exe OR *\WSCRIPT.EXE OR *\cscript.exe OR *\CScript.exe OR *\CSCRIPT.EXE) @ParentCommandLine:(*"\\Users\\Public\\Documents\\"* AND *".js"*) @Image:(*\curl.exe OR *\CURL.EXE OR *\schtasks.exe OR *\SCHTASKS.EXE OR *\cmd.exe OR *\CMD.EXE OR *\powershell.exe OR *\POWERSHELL.EXE OR *\pwsh.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ParentBaseFileName=/(wscript|cscript)\.exe$/i

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK

Match SHA256/SHA1/MD5 named in the article against EDR file/process telemetry.

Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes DeviceFileEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Pre-filter each table BEFORE the union — the engine cannot push
// predicates across `union`, and DeviceFileEvents lacks ProcessCommandLine
// (Initiating only) so column-projection has to differ per side.
union
    ( DeviceFileEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = InitiatingProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceFileEvents" ),
    ( DeviceProcessEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(7d)
        | where AccountName !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or SHA1 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8") or MD5 in~ ("7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8")
        | project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256,
                  Cmd = ProcessCommandLine, Source = "DeviceProcessEvents" )
| order by Timestamp desc

// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["7630debd35cac6b7d58c4427695579b3e3a8b1cc462f523234cd6c698882a68c", "a7abf1d9d6686af1cefcd60b17a312e7eb8cfe267def1ec34aeab6128c811630", "23c1e673f315dafa14b73034a90dd3d393a984451ff6601b8be8142be6487b43", "cf9fc891ea5ca5ecd8113ef3e69f6f52ff538b6cccbdaa9559106fc72bc6da30", "100407796028bf3649752d9d2a67a0e4394d752eb8de86daa42920e814f3fae8"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

HAPI FHIR XXE: DOCTYPE/ENTITY SYSTEM payload posted to FHIR endpoint (CVE-2026-55471) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR API paths whose XML body carries XXE markers (<!DOCTYPE … <!ENTITY … SYSTEM 'file://' or 'http://'). Targets the entry-point of CVE-2026-55471 where attacker-controlled XML is fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform with an unhardened Saxon TransformerFactory. Rationale: Article specifies the entry point is XML fed to XsltUtilities.saxonTransform; PoC literally shows '<!DOCTYPE root [' + '<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://..."' + '<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://..."'. FHIR URL fragments come from standard HAPI deployments. Corroborated via vulnerability.circl.lu GHSA-2F55-G35J-5JMF entry. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.001
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Internal Burp/ZAP/Nuclei scans hitting FHIR endpoints with XXE payloads as part of authorized AppSec testing
  • Legitimate FHIR XML payloads that include a benign internal DOCTYPE (rare but possible for IG packages)
  • Health-IT interop tools that embed XSD references via DOCTYPE during conformance testing
  • WAF echo-back / debug logs that quote the original payload back into the log line
Suppression filter
| where RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap","Acunetix") and SourceIP !in ("<known_scanner_ips>")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Pull the full request body and confirm an external SYSTEM identifier (file://, http://, https://, jar:, netdoc:). Map the destination FHIR endpoint to its backing JVM/container and check whether HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 is present. 2) CONTAIN — Block the source IP at the WAF, drop any in-flight session, and add a virtual patch rule that rejects FHIR POST/PUT bodies containing <!DOCTYPE or <!ENTITY. If exploitation confirmed, isolate the FHIR app server and rotate any local secrets the JVM could read. 3) HUNT — Pivot on the source IP across the last 30d for other FHIR endpoints and parameter-entity variants (UC2). Pull DeviceFileEvents on the JVM host for /etc/passwd, application.properties, ~/.aws/credentials reads (UC3). Pull DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound HTTP/DNS from java.exe to the attacker-controlled OOB domain (UC4).
// Defender XDR does not capture HTTP request bodies; pivot is the FHIR endpoint URL hit (DeviceNetworkEvents shows the host:port + URL fragment only). Pair with WAF logs in Sentinel (sentinel_kql below) for body inspection.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted" or ActionType == "ConnectionInbound"
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe","tomcat.exe","tomcat9.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, LocalPort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
let XxeMarkers = dynamic(["<!DOCTYPE","<!ENTITY","SYSTEM \"file:","SYSTEM \"http:","SYSTEM 'file:","SYSTEM 'http:"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend BodyCandidates = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString2), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString3), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString4), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString5), "|", tostring(DeviceCustomString6), "|", tostring(RequestContext), "|", tostring(Message))
| where BodyCandidates has_any (XxeMarkers)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestMethod, RequestClientApplication, BodyExcerpt = substring(BodyCandidates, 0, 1024), DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: HAPI FHIR XXE Payload in HTTP Body (CVE-2026-55471)
id: 8e2a0c14-9e7f-4d5a-bf3e-5471a55471aa
status: experimental
description: Detects inbound HTTP POST/PUT to FHIR endpoints whose body contains XML External Entity declarations, the entry vector for CVE-2026-55471 in HAPI FHIR XsltUtilities.saxonTransform.
references:
  - https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
  - https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/18
tags:
  - attack.initial_access
  - attack.t1190
  - attack.t1071.001
logsource:
  category: webserver
detection:
  selection_method:
    cs-method:
      - POST
      - PUT
  selection_path:
    cs-uri-stem|contains:
      - '/fhir/'
      - '/hl7/fhir/'
      - '/baseR4/'
      - '/baseDstu3/'
      - '/StructureDefinition'
      - '/ValueSet'
  selection_body:
    cs-body|contains:
      - '<!DOCTYPE'
      - '<!ENTITY'
      - 'SYSTEM "file:'
      - 'SYSTEM "http:'
  condition: selection_method and selection_path and selection_body
falsepositives:
  - Legitimate FHIR clients using internal DTDs (rare in modern FHIR XML)
  - Security scanners (Burp, ZAP, Nuclei) testing the same endpoints
level: high
(@http.method:(POST OR PUT)) (@http.url_details.path:(*\/fhir\/* OR *\/hl7\/fhir\/* OR *\/baseR4\/* OR *\/baseDstu3\/* OR *\/StructureDefinition* OR *\/ValueSet*)) (@http.request.body:(*"<!DOCTYPE"* OR *"<!ENTITY"* OR *"SYSTEM \"file:"* OR *"SYSTEM \"http:"*))
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method in ("POST","PUT") (Web.url="*/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/hl7/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/baseR4/*" OR Web.url="*/baseDstu3/*" OR Web.url="*/StructureDefinition*" OR Web.url="*/ValueSet*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user Web.http_user_agent _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search _raw="*<!DOCTYPE*" OR _raw="*<!ENTITY*SYSTEM*" | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<xxe_marker><!ENTITY[^>]+SYSTEM\s+[\"'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):[^\"']+[\"'])" | where isnotnull(xxe_marker) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Web.Web where Web.http_method in ("POST","PUT") (Web.url="*/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/hl7/fhir/*" OR Web.url="*/baseR4/*" OR Web.url="*/baseDstu3/*" OR Web.url="*/StructureDefinition*" OR Web.url="*/ValueSet*") by Web.src Web.dest Web.url Web.http_method Web.user Web.http_user_agent _raw | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | search _raw="*<!DOCTYPE*" OR _raw="*<!ENTITY*SYSTEM*" | rex field=_raw "(?i)(?<xxe_marker><!ENTITY[^>]+SYSTEM\s+[\"'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):[^\"']+[\"'])" | where isnotnull(xxe_marker) | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
HAPI FHIR XXE: parameter-entity (<!ENTITY %) OOB exfil pattern on FHIR endpoint AIExploitation High
Higher-fidelity sibling of the generic DOCTYPE hunt: matches only payloads that declare a parameter entity (<!ENTITY %) with an external SYSTEM identifier, the exact pattern used for blind XXE / SSRF in the article's PoC. Parameter entities are vanishingly rare in benign FHIR traffic. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` to set up OOB exfil — the parameter-entity construct (`%`) is the distinguishing signature of XXE-via-DTD attacks and almost never appears in legitimate FHIR XML. Much lower-FP than UC1's generic DOCTYPE/ENTITY hunt. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190 T1071.004
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized AppSec scanning by internal red team / Burp Pro extensions
  • Bug-bounty researcher probing exposed FHIR test environments
  • FHIR conformance test harnesses that embed parameter entities in edge-case test vectors (extremely rare)
  • Researcher proof-of-concepts in pre-prod where the source IP belongs to an internal pentest range
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in ("<internal_appsec_scanner_ips>") and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Burp","ZAP","Nuclei","sqlmap")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — This signature is high-fidelity; treat any hit as exploitation attempt until proven otherwise. Capture the full Body, the source IP, the targeted FHIR resource path, and the parent JVM hostname. Confirm HAPI FHIR version on the receiver. 2) CONTAIN — Block source IP at WAF immediately. Apply ModSecurity / WAF rule to drop any inbound XML containing `<!ENTITY %` for FHIR endpoints regardless of upgrade status. Snapshot the JVM heap if exploit may have succeeded so artefacts can be retrieved later. 3) HUNT — Pivot to UC4 (java.exe outbound to the OOB callback domain in the SYSTEM URI) and UC3 (java.exe reading sensitive local files). Search the WAF for the same source IP over 30d on any FHIR-shaped path. Cross-check the OOB host/IP against threat-intel feeds and add to the Sentinel ThreatIntelligenceIndicator table.
// Defender XDR has no HTTP body visibility; this detection lives in WAF/proxy logs surfaced through Sentinel. The Defender query below is the host-side companion: JVM serving FHIR that immediately performs an outbound HTTP fetch to a public IP (the parameter-entity callback).
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","javaw.exe")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where RemotePort in (80, 443, 8080, 8443)
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","tomcat","jetty","spring-boot","wildfly")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
let FhirPaths = dynamic(["/fhir/","/hl7/fhir/","/baseR4/","/baseDstu3/","/StructureDefinition","/ValueSet","/metadata"]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where RequestMethod in ("POST","PUT")
| where RequestURL has_any (FhirPaths)
| extend Body = strcat(tostring(DeviceCustomString1),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString2),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString3),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString4),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString5),"|",tostring(DeviceCustomString6),"|",tostring(RequestContext),"|",tostring(Message))
| where Body matches regex @"(?i)<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'](?:file|http|https|ftp|jar|netdoc|gopher):"
| extend ParamEntity = extract(@"(?i)(<!ENTITY\s+%\s+\w+\s+SYSTEM\s+[""'][^""']+[""'])", 1, Body)
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, ParamEntity, BodyExcerpt = substring(Body, 0, 1024)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

JVM serving HAPI FHIR reads sensitive local files (XXE file:// disclosure) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects post-exploitation file reads by the JVM hosting HAPI FHIR: /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow, /etc/hosts, application.properties, application.yml, cloud credentials, and Kubernetes secrets. Catches the file:// SYSTEM-entity arm of CVE-2026-55471 regardless of whether the inbound WAF caught the payload. Rationale: Article's PoC uses `<!ENTITY canary SYSTEM "file://...">` to read a temp file containing `TOP-SECRET-FHIR-XSLT-CANARY-3f9a17c2`. Real attackers will pivot to /etc/passwd, application.properties (DB creds), and cloud-credential files. JVM as the reader + Java-app-server cmdline narrows scope. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of the file-disclosure exploitation primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1005 T1083 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR legitimately loading its own application.yml / hapi.properties from its install directory at startup
  • Spring Boot Actuator config refresh reading application config
  • Backup/snapshot tooling that crawls the FHIR app directory and triggers file-access events on config
  • Sysadmin running diagnostic tools (strace, jstack against the JVM) that incidentally surface as the JVM touching these files
Suppression filter
| where not (FolderPath endswith "hapi.properties" and FolderPath startswith "/opt/hapi-fhir/") and not (FolderPath endswith "application.yml" and FolderPath has "/conf/")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the JVM in question is the FHIR app server (check parent process tree, listening ports, classpath). Pull the timestamp of the file read and look ±60s in CommonSecurityLog / Web datamodel for an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint (UC1/UC2). 2) CONTAIN — Stop the JVM, snapshot heap + thread dump, isolate the host from network. Rotate every secret the JVM could read (application.properties DB creds, AWS access keys, K8s service-account tokens, SSH keys). 3) HUNT — Run UC4 to look for OOB exfil of the file contents to attacker-controlled domains. Search the same JVM hosts for inbound traffic to FHIR endpoints from the source IP over the past 30d. Apply the WAF virtual-patch from UC2 to every FHIR-fronting WAF.

DeviceFileEvents

| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java.exe","java","javaw.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("hapi","org.hl7.fhir","hapi-fhir","tomcat","jetty","wildfly","spring-boot")
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileRenamed","FileModified","FileAccessed","FileOpened")
| where FolderPath has_any (SensitivePaths)
| where not (FolderPath has_any ("target/classes","/opt/hapi-fhir/conf/application.yml","<known_legitimate_config_paths>"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ActionType, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc

HAPI FHIR JVM out-of-band callback to non-corporate destination (XXE OOB exfil) AICommand & Control Medium
Detects the SSRF / blind-XXE arm of CVE-2026-55471: the FHIR-serving JVM makes an outbound HTTP fetch or DNS lookup to a public destination it has never previously contacted, immediately after an inbound POST/PUT to a FHIR endpoint. Captures both the parameter-entity DTD fetch and the file-content exfil pattern. Rationale: PoC sets up `<!ENTITY % oob SYSTEM "http://127.0.0.1:port/evil-fhir-xslt-ssrf.dtd">` and the JVM resolves it, generating an outbound HTTP request from the Saxon TransformerFactory. Real attackers replace 127.0.0.1 with attacker.com. Anti-join against 30d baseline turns 'JVM made an HTTP request' into 'JVM contacted a destination it never contacted before'. Corroborated against vulnerability.circl.lu confirmation of SSRF primitive. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1041 T1071.001 T1071.004 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • HAPI FHIR pulling new external IG (Implementation Guide) packages from a registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net)
  • JVM auto-update / Maven Central / Spring Boot Actuator phoning home
  • Newly-onboarded healthcare partner whose endpoint URL is genuinely contacted for the first time
  • Container image rebuilds that change the destination set seen at runtime
Suppression filter
| where not (RemoteUrl has_any ("registry.fhir.org","packages.simplifier.net","packages2.fhir.org","repo.maven.apache.org","repo1.maven.org","jcenter.bintray.com"))
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the destination domain/IP is not a known FHIR registry (registry.fhir.org, packages.simplifier.net, packages2.fhir.org). Look at the immediate-prior inbound HTTP requests to the JVM (CommonSecurityLog / W3CIISLog within 60s before the outbound) for FHIR endpoint POST/PUT carrying the matching attacker domain in a SYSTEM identifier. 2) CONTAIN — If the destination is an attacker callback, block it at egress firewall + add to ThreatIntelligenceIndicator. Rotate any secrets that may have been leaked over the channel (assume worst case — UC3 enumerates targets). 3) HUNT — Pivot on the attacker destination across all JVM hosts in the estate over the past 30d. Pull the file-read events from UC3 in the same time window. Check whether the attacker domain appears in DNS logs from other hosts (lateral targeting).

Vulnerable HAPI FHIR org.hl7.fhir.utilities < 6.9.10 in software inventory (CVE-2026-55471) AIReconnaissance High
Inventory pivot: lists every host running HAPI FHIR with the vulnerable org.hl7.fhir.utilities Maven artifact (< 6.9.10). Drives patching and tells the SOC which hosts to prioritise for the runtime detections (UC1-UC4) until upgraded. Rationale: Article pins the vulnerable artifact (`ca.uhn.hapi.fhir:org.hl7.fhir.utilities`) and the vulnerable file:line (XsltUtilities.java:61/91/106 in <= 6.9.8). Web search confirmed the fix landed in 6.9.10, so the vulnerable range is < 6.9.10. CveId match is the cleanest inventory pivot and directly drives patch prioritisation + scopes UC1-UC4 to the right hosts. Cross-checked against: • https://vulnerability.circl.lu/vuln/ghsa-2f55-g35j-5jmf • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-2f55-g35j-5jmf
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesVulnerabilities.Vulnerabilities
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Test / lab hosts intentionally running old HAPI FHIR for compatibility testing
  • Containers pinned to a vulnerable version because of an unrelated downstream dependency conflict — true positive for inventory but not actionable until refactor
  • TVM lag — DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities may not enumerate Java JARs unless the agent indexes them; results may under-report
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE — Confirm the host is actually serving FHIR (listening on a FHIR endpoint, not just a build artifact). Capture HAPI FHIR base version + org.hl7.fhir.utilities version. 2) CONTAIN — For internet-facing FHIR hosts: deploy the UC2 WAF rule (block `<!ENTITY %`) as virtual patch. Schedule emergency upgrade to org.hl7.fhir.utilities >= 6.9.10. 3) HUNT — Enable UC1-UC4 with elevated priority for the listed hosts. Backsearch CommonSecurityLog 30d for any FHIR POST/PUT with XXE markers targeting these hosts. Pull DeviceFileEvents for any sensitive-file read by their JVM (UC3).

Unauthenticated POST to Langflow /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} endpoint (CVE-2026-55450) AIDelivery High
Detects HTTP POST traffic to the deprecated, unauthenticated Langflow upload endpoint exploited by CVE-2026-55450. Hunts the exact URI pattern reachable on the default Langflow port 7860 where any UUID is accepted and no Authorization header is required. Rationale: Article explicitly names POST /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} as the unauthenticated endpoint and shows the curl PoC against port 7860. Cross-checked GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735 advisory and PR #12831 confirming the endpoint path and Langflow default port. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831

Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users on internal network triggering uploads via the deprecated endpoint pre-1.9.1
  • Internal QA/CI pipelines testing Langflow upload functionality
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, Burp) probing the endpoint
  • Authorized red-team / pentest engagements
  • Self-hosted internal Langflow instances reached by power users via curl
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (<internal_qa_subnet>, <vuln_scanner_ips>) and RequestClientApplication !has_any ("Nessus","Qualys","Burp")
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the target host is running Langflow <1.9.1; check /api/v1/version. Validate source IP — internal/known user vs external/unknown. Pull the response body to see if file_path was disclosed. Step 2 (contain): Block external traffic to TCP/7860 at the perimeter; if Langflow is exposed publicly, push WAF rule blocking POST /api/v1/upload/. Patch to Langflow 1.9.1+. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on source IP for follow-on activity (other Langflow endpoints, scanning behaviour, exfil). Check Langflow cache directory size; look for atypical file extensions written to /var/cache/langflow/ or ~/.cache/langflow/.

Langflow upload volume spike — disk-exhaustion DoS pattern (CVE-2026-55450) AIActions on Objectives High
Detects abuse of the unauthenticated Langflow upload endpoint at scale — many POSTs to /api/v1/upload/ from one source within a short window, indicating space-exhaustion DoS exploitation. Threshold-based, alerting tier. Rationale: Article: 'Unauthenticated users can upload any amount of data to the server without any limitations... can lead to space exhaustion on the server.' Threshold tuned for repeated POSTs to the named endpoint. 1.9.1 patch enforces max_file_size_upload returning HTTP 413, supporting the volume-based abuse model. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831
ATT&CKT1499.001
Data sourcesWeb
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate bulk-ingest of training documents by power users
  • Langflow CI/CD test suite that exercises the upload endpoint repeatedly
  • Backup/restore tooling re-uploading flow assets
  • Load testing or capacity planning runs
  • Misconfigured client retrying after 413 responses post-patch

| where SourceIP !in (<internal_qa_subnet>, <internal_loadtest_subnet>)

Step 1 (triage): Confirm source IP is external/unknown; check df -h or equivalent on Langflow host for cache-volume utilisation jump. Sample 3-5 of the recorded requests to confirm same URI shape. Step 2 (contain): Rate-limit or block source IP at WAF/firewall; if disk >85%, clear /var/cache/langflow/ (or ~/.cache/langflow/). Restart Langflow if hung. Patch to 1.9.1+. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on source IP for scans against other Langflow paths or other CVE-2026-55450 targets in the org. Search for the same IP hitting other internal AI/ML tooling.

Rapid file growth in Langflow cache directory (CVE-2026-55450 disk exhaustion) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Detects an unusual rate of file writes under the Langflow cache directory — the artefact of unauthenticated upload abuse. Targets the cache paths named in the advisory (`~/Library/Caches/langflow/`, `~/.cache/langflow/`, `/var/cache/langflow/`). Rationale: Article PoC shows files written to `/Users/ori/Library/Caches/langflow/<flow_id>/<sha>.<ext>`. The advisory describes attackers uploading without limits — disk exhaustion materialises as a burst of writes inside the Langflow cache dir, which is the host-side observable of the attack. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735

Langflow upload response leaks absolute cache path (CVE-2026-55450 info disclosure) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects HTTP responses from /api/v1/upload/ that include an absolute filesystem path in the response body — the exact information-leak primitive the advisory describes. Pivots on the `file_path` JSON field with `/Caches/langflow/`, `/.cache/langflow/`, or `/var/cache/langflow/` substrings. Rationale: Article: 'in the response, the absolute path of the uploaded file is reported to the attacker, which is an information leak that can assist in chaining other primitives.' PoC response shows `"file_path":"/Users/ori/Library/Caches/langflow/.../...txt"`. Detection keys on the literal JSON field name plus the cache-path substring. Requires WAF/proxy with response-body capture. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735

Even post-patch the path still leaks to the owner — consider PR follow-up to return relative paths only. Step 3 (hunt): Search for the disclosed username/home-directory pattern in other attack surfaces — same user enumerated via other Langflow endpoints, SSH attempts, etc.

Correlated Langflow upload burst with cache-directory write spike AIActions on Objectives High
Joins inbound POSTs to /api/v1/upload/{flow_id} with simultaneous file-create bursts under the Langflow cache directory on the same host within a 5-minute window. Confirms the upload→storage chain and rules out unrelated cache churn. Rationale: Reviewer feedback request: tuple-correlate upload burst with cache write burst on same host within 2-5min. Article gives exact URI and exact cache directory pattern; pairing them eliminates background cache churn FPs. Cross-checked PR #12831 — the fix path (save_uploaded_file → folder_name=flow_id_str) confirms the host-side directory shape. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831

Successful Langflow /api/* request with missing Authorization header (unauth API access) AIReconnaissance Medium
Detects HTTP 200/201/204 responses to /api/* paths on Langflow hosts where the Authorization header is absent or empty — the broader unauthenticated-access pattern implied by the advisory. Excludes known unauth health endpoints. Rationale: Reviewer feedback + article text: 'Unauthenticated users can upload any amount of data... only network access to Langflow' implies the auth gap may affect other deprecated endpoints. Detection covers /api/ surface area with explicit health-endpoint exclusions and missing-Authorization check. Cross-checked PR #12831 which adds `get_flow` dependency — confirming the missing-auth shape is the root cause class. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-x223-p2gf-v735 • https://github.com/langflow-ai/langflow/pull/12831

Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Langflow public docs/static endpoints that legitimately need no auth
  • Reverse proxy that strips Authorization header before forwarding
  • SSO/OIDC flows using cookies rather than Bearer tokens
  • Front-end fetches hitting backend with session cookies
  • Internal monitoring probes hitting undocumented unauth endpoints
Suppression filter
| where SourceIP !in (<internal_monitoring_subnet>) and not(Paths has_any ("/api/v1/docs","/api/v1/openapi.json","/api/v1/auto_login"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm Langflow version (<1.9.1 is vulnerable). Enumerate the specific /api/ paths hit — cross-check against Langflow source for which require auth. Identify source IP attribution. Step 2 (contain): If unauth endpoints other than the known exclusions are reachable externally, restrict at WAF/firewall or via reverse-proxy auth gate. Upgrade to 1.9.1+ which adds get_flow auth dependency. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot source IP and look for follow-on actions — upload attempts, flow enumeration, credential probing on adjacent services.
